sections.title: Mental model — Big-O, Θ, Ω as promises

blocks.md: **O(f)**: *won't grow meaningfully faster than f* (upper promise). **Ω(f)**: *at least f on some inputs* (lower promise). **Θ(f)**: *exactly the f family* (tight). Interviews say "complexity?" and expect Θ-style answers with O vocabulary.

rows.label: "Bubble sort is Ω(n)"
rows.left: can't beat one pass (must inspect all) ✓

rows.label: "Counting inversions via mergesort is Θ(n log n)"
rows.left: tightly n log n in AND out

rows.label: "Quicksort is O(n²) but usually Θ(n log n)"
rows.left: worst-case ceiling differs from typical behavior

items: **Sequential blocks ADD**: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²) — the biggest term owns the total
**Nested loops MULTIPLY**, but inner bound may shrink (`j<i` triangle ≈ n²/2 → still Θ(n²))
**Recursion**: count tree nodes × per-node work. Halving depth + linear merge = T(n)=2T(n/2)+n ⇒ Θ(n log n)
**Amortized**: rare spikes averaged over a sequence (vector growth) — quote as amortized O(1)

items.explain: One subproblem, half size, constant work per level → levels = log n.

items.explain: Half of n² still lives in the n² family.

blocks.md: Memorize this table cold — interviewers probe whether you know what each container CHARGES:

segments.name: vector · random access O(1)
segments.desc: push_back amortized O(1) · insert/erase middle O(n) · sort member-free

segments.name: stack / queue
segments.desc: adapter over deque — all core ops O(1)

segments.name: priority_queue
segments.desc: push/pop Θ(log n) · top O(1) · NO decrease-key

segments.desc: insert/erase/find Θ(log n) · ITERATED IN SORTED ORDER

blocks.label: algorithms that ride on sorted order
blocks.code:
vector<int> v = {5, 2, 8, 2};
sort(v.begin(), v.end());                 // 2 2 5 8

bool exists = binary_search(v.begin(), v.end(), 5);   // true
auto lo = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);  // first >= 2 -> idx0
auto up = upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);  // first >  2 -> idx2
cout << up - lo;                          // COUNT of 2s = 2

// rotate, reverse, accumulate:
cout << accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);   // sum, ll accumulator!
cout << __builtin_popcount(13);                // bits: 3
blocks.py:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
v = sorted([5, 2, 8, 2])          # [2,2,5,8]

lo = bisect_left(v, 2)            # first >= 2 -> 0
up = bisect_right(v, 2)           # first > 2  -> 2
print(up - lo)                    # count of 2s = 2

print(sum(v))                     # accumulate
print(bin(13).count('1'))         # popcount equivalent

sections.title: Problem set — L2 ladder (container choice + analysis)

items.title: Two Sum
items.statement: Indices of two numbers summing to target. Solve O(n) with unordered_map; explain the naive O(n²) you avoided.
hints: For each x ask map: seen target−x?
Insert AFTER checking to avoid self-pair.

solutionCode.label: ask the map before inserting

items.complexity: Time O(n) average — one pass, one hash probe each. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why insert after checking rather than before?
followups.a: Inserting first lets an element pair with itself. With target 6 and nums [3,2,4], index 0 would find its own 3 already in the map and return [0,0]. Checking first guarantees the partner came from a strictly earlier index.

followups.q: What did the hash map buy over the naive solution?
followups.a: The naive double loop is O(n²) — 10^10 operations at n = 10^5. The map turns "is the complement present?" from a scan into a single probe, giving O(n) time for O(n) space. It also assumes good hashing; adversarial keys can degrade it to O(n²) worst case.

items.title: Contains Duplicate
items.statement: Any value twice? Then discuss why sort+scan also passes and compare costs.
hints: Set insert returns pair<it,bool>.
Sort route: adjacent equals after Θ(n log n).

solutionCode.label: set membership, early exit

items.complexity: Set: O(n) average time, O(n) space. Sort+scan: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

followups.q: When would you prefer sort-and-scan?
followups.a: When memory is tight or the array is already sorted. Sorting is O(n log n) but uses O(1) extra space, and duplicates then sit adjacent so one pass finds them. It also gives worst-case guarantees, whereas hashing is only average-case O(n).

followups.q: What does `seen.insert(x).second` return?
followups.a: std::set and unordered_set insert return a pair of (iterator, bool), where the bool is true if the element was newly added. So `!...second` means "it was already there" — a single operation that both probes and inserts, avoiding a redundant lookup.

items.title: Valid Anagram
items.statement: Same letters same counts? Use 26-array; then say when you'd switch to unordered_map.
hints: Increment for s, decrement for t, check zeros.
Unicode/arbitrary chars → hash map instead.

solutionCode.label: increment for s, decrement for t, expect all zeros

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) — the 26-slot array is fixed size regardless of input length.

followups.q: Why is the 26-array O(1) space?
followups.a: Its size depends on the alphabet, not on n. Whether the strings are 10 or 10 million characters, it stays 26 ints. Space complexity measures growth with input size, and this does not grow.

followups.q: When do you switch to a hash map?
followups.a: The moment the alphabet stops being small and contiguous — Unicode, arbitrary bytes, or case-sensitive mixed input. An array indexed by code point would need over a million slots for Unicode; a hash map holds only the characters actually present.

items.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
items.statement: Unique common elements — implement with unordered_set; state complexities of both build and probe phases.
hints: Set the smaller array; scan larger against it.
Result uniqueness: erase on match or second set.

solutionCode.label: hash the smaller array, probe with the larger

items.complexity: Time O(n + m) average. Space O(min(n, m)) if you hash the smaller array.

followups.q: Why does erasing on match give uniqueness for free?
followups.a: The first time a value is seen in the larger array it is present in the set, gets recorded, and is removed. Every later occurrence probes a set that no longer contains it, so it is skipped. No second set or post-pass dedup is needed.

followups.q: Separate the build and probe costs.
followups.a: Building the set is O(min(n,m)) inserts. Probing is O(max(n,m)) lookups. Total O(n + m) average. Hashing the smaller side matters for space, not time — it caps memory at the smaller of the two.

items.title: Missing Number
items.statement: [0..n] with one missing. Sum-formula AND XOR solutions; watch overflow reasoning.
hints: Expected sum n(n+1)/2 minus actual — use long long.
XOR route: pairs cancel, survivor is answer.

solutionCode.label: sum formula and the XOR alternative

items.complexity: Both O(n) time, O(1) space. XOR avoids overflow entirely.

followups.q: Where is the overflow risk in the sum version?
followups.a: n(n+1)/2 for n = 10^5 is about 5×10^9, past the 32-bit signed limit of 2.1×10^9. Computing it in int overflows before the subtraction. Widening to 64 bits fixes it — this is precisely why the XOR version is considered safer.

followups.q: Why does XOR work?
followups.a: XOR is its own inverse and is commutative, so a ^ a = 0 and order does not matter. XORing all indices 0..n together with all present values cancels every matched pair, leaving only the index whose value is absent — the missing number.

items.title: Merge Sorted Array (in-place)
items.statement: nums1 has trailing space; merge nums2 without extra buffer.
hints: Fill from the BACK with three pointers.
Largest goes last — avoids overwriting unread data.

solutionCode.label: fill from the back so nothing unread is overwritten

items.complexity: Time O(n + m). Space O(1) — the merge happens in nums1 trailing space.

followups.q: Why fill from the back?
followups.a: The spare capacity is at the end. Writing forward from index 0 would clobber nums1 entries that have not been read yet. Writing backward always targets a slot that is either empty space or an element already consumed, so nothing is lost.

followups.q: Why does the loop condition only check j?
followups.a: If nums2 is exhausted, whatever remains in nums1 is already in its correct final position — it never needed moving. If nums1 runs out first, the `i >= 0` guard sends the remaining nums2 values through. Looping on `i >= 0 || j >= 0` also works but does needless self-copies.

items.title: Kth Smallest in Array
items.statement: kth smallest via sort AND via heap; compare costs aloud (n log n vs n log k).
hints: Heap route: keep size-k MAX-heap, pop on overflow.
Answer sits at pq.top() at the end.

solutionCode.label: size-k max-heap: evict whenever it overflows

items.complexity: Sort: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra. Size-k max-heap: O(n log k) time, O(k) space — better when k is small.

followups.q: Why a MAX-heap for the k SMALLEST?
followups.a: You need instant access to the worst element currently kept, so you can evict it when a better candidate arrives. The worst of the k smallest is the largest, so the heap must surface the maximum. It also means the answer — the kth smallest — is sitting at the top when you finish.

followups.q: When is sorting still the better answer?
followups.a: When k is close to n, since n log k approaches n log n and sorting has far better constants and no allocation. Also when you need several different k values from the same data — sort once, index many times.

items.title: Next Greater Element
items.statement: First greater to the right for each element (circular-free version). Stack+map pipeline.
hints: Walk right-to-left; pop smaller tops.
Store answers in value→value map for query phase.

solutionCode.label: monotonic stack right-to-left, answers stored by value

items.complexity: Time O(n + m) — each element is pushed and popped at most once. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why can a popped element never be needed again?
followups.a: Scanning right-to-left, if st.top() ≤ current then for anything further left the current element is both nearer and at least as large. The popped value can never be the *first* greater element for any future query, so discarding it is permanently safe.

followups.q: Why store answers keyed by value rather than index?
followups.a: The problem guarantees nums2 has distinct values and nums1 is a subset of it, so a value is a valid unique key. With duplicates this breaks and you would have to map indices and locate each nums1 element in nums2 first.

items.title: Sort by Length (comparator drill)
items.statement: Sort strings ascending by length; equal lengths keep original relative order — justify stable_sort vs sort here.
hints: Stability matters ONLY because tie-order must persist.
Lambda comparing sizes; strict `<` only.

solutionCode.label: stable_sort with a strict comparator on length only

items.complexity: O(n log n) comparisons. stable_sort may allocate O(n) scratch; sort is in-place but unstable.

followups.q: Why stable_sort rather than sort here?
followups.a: The requirement says equal-length strings must keep their original relative order. std::sort gives no such guarantee — it may permute equal elements arbitrarily. Stability is only worth its cost when tie order is part of the specification, which it is here.

followups.q: What breaks if the comparator returns `a.size() <= b.size()`?
followups.a: It stops being a strict weak ordering: the comparator would report that two equal-length strings each precede the other. libstdc++ uses the comparator as a loop guard while partitioning, so it can run past the end of the array — undefined behaviour, typically a crash, and only on inputs containing ties.

items.title: Range Count Queries
items.statement: Sorted array, q queries [a,b]: how many elements inside? Must be O(log n) per query.
hints: upper_bound(b) − lower_bound(a).
Never rescan per query — that's O(nq).

solutionCode.label: bracket the range with lower_bound and upper_bound
solutionCode.py:
import bisect


def count_in_range(a: list[int], lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    """a must be sorted. Counts values in the inclusive range [lo, hi]."""
    left = bisect.bisect_left(a, lo)    # first >= lo
    right = bisect.bisect_right(a, hi)  # first > hi
    return max(0, right - left)         # inverted range => 0, never negative

items.complexity: O(log n) per query after an O(n log n) sort. Total O(n log n + q log n) instead of O(n·q).

followups.q: Why lower_bound for the left edge but upper_bound for the right?
followups.a: The range is inclusive. lower_bound(lo) is the first element not less than lo, so it includes lo itself. upper_bound(hi) is the first element strictly greater than hi, so subtracting gives a half-open span that counts hi. Using lower_bound on both ends would drop every copy of hi.

followups.q: Why is rescanning per query unacceptable?
followups.a: With n and q both 10^5, an O(n) scan per query is 10^10 operations. Sorting once and binary searching makes it about 10^5·17 ≈ 2×10^6. The sort is paid once; the queries become effectively free.

followups.q: What does an inverted query (lo > hi) return?
followups.a: Zero — but only because of the explicit clamp. Without it, lower_bound(lo) can land past upper_bound(hi) and the subtraction yields a negative count, which silently corrupts any running total the caller keeps. Guard the empty range rather than assuming callers validate it.

Recurrence intuition: halving+linear work ⇒ Θ(n log n); halving+constant ⇒ Θ(log n)

map/tree Θ(log n)+sorted iteration · unordered avg O(1)+rehash storms+no order

Comparator must be strict (<) — never <= inside sort

glossary.def: Upper ceiling / tight bound / floor on growth family.
Sequence-average cost after spreading rare expensive operations.
Bucket-array regrowth re-placing every element; invalidates iterators.
First-not-less / first-greater positions in sorted ranges — bracket queries.
std::sort's hybrid (quick+heap+insertion) guaranteeing Θ(n log n) worst case.
Preserves original order of equal keys (stable_sort, merge-based).
Lowering a heap item's priority in place — std::priority_queue lacks it; design around it.
